description: Kafala transfers control of a migrant worker's immigration and employment status to the individual employer. Legally a worker cannot leave the country without the employer's permission, even when experiencing abuse - so reporting to local authorities is rarely an option.
energy_note: You may not leave the country without his signature.

description: Young Nigerian women are recruited as housekeepers by registered agencies in Nigeria, with contracts reportedly stipulating that for the first 24 months they cannot ask for a salary increase, stop work, run away, or refuse to finish the contract.
time_note: The period during which she may not stop.
energy_note: Two years in which quitting is a breach of contract.

aspect: The conditions, from a survey of fifty
description: In one survey of 50 women migrants, all worked seven-day weeks and all had passports confiscated; many reported violence and sexual abuse, and most had paid recruitment fees. Employers cover travel and documentation costs and use that as leverage; agencies profit further by auctioning workers' contracts online.
energy_note: Fifty out of fifty, seven days a week, no passport.

description: In August 2018 two Nigerian migrant domestic staff were killed in Riyadh by their Saudi employers.
energy_note: Two women, named in a report, killed by the household they worked in.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the eight who were not allowed to board
description: In May 2020, 50 trafficked Nigerian women returned from Lebanon along with 19 nationals stranded by COVID-19 restrictions - but activists reported eight women were blocked from boarding, their employers refusing permission to leave and alleging the women had stolen from them.
energy_note: Rescue flight on the runway, and eight of them not allowed on it.

aspect: Being abandoned is a distinct outcome from being abused
description: Migrants abandoned by their sponsors can be stranded for years because they cannot afford a return flight. Not employed, not deported, not able to leave.
energy_note: Left, in a country she cannot leave.

aspect: The newer destination, with no embassy
description: NAPTIP first flagged exploitative recruitment drives to Iraq in May 2023. There is no Nigerian embassy there, so it coordinates through the consulate in Jordan. Several Nigerian women remain in detention for offences including conflicts with employers and overstaying residence permits.
energy_note: Detained in a country where her own government has no office.

description: The IOM has documented roughly a 600% increase in potential sex trafficking victims arriving from Africa to the Gulf states in recent decades, with abuse incidents mainly in Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.
energy_note: A sixfold increase, and a legal framework that enables it.
